match.reason: None of the bank points teaches weighing the short- and long-term effects of an economic decision on different groups; the closest, short-term and long-term objectives, is a Year 12 business planning idea about time frames for objectives, not evaluation of effects.

draft.title: Short-term and long-term effects
card: Short-term effects happen soon after a decision. Long-term effects show up months or years later. The two can be quite different.
A decision can help now and cost later, or cost now and help later. Borrowing to study costs money now and repayments later, but a qualification may lead to higher pay.
Effects also fall on different groups, such as borrowers, workers, taxpayers or businesses. A good result for one group may be a poor result for another.
To judge a decision, list its effects over time and for each group. Then compare them, rather than looking only at the first result.
draft.remember: Weigh effects over time and across groups, not just the first result.

a.q: Which example is a decision that helps now but is likely to cost later?
opts: Skipping repairs to save money, then paying bigger bills
Saving part of each pay to buy a car in two years
Paying for a trade course, then earning more later
Training staff at a café, so that service improves over time
a.why: Skipping repairs saves money now, but the damage can grow and cost more later. The trade course is the reverse: it costs now and may pay off later.
a.clue: Look for the benefit coming first and the cost second.

b.q: A council in Tasmania cuts a local tax to help shops now, but must later cut road repairs. How should the decision be judged?
opts: List effects now and later for shops, drivers and ratepayers
Judge it only by the extra money shops gain this year
Judge it only by what happens to roads in ten years
Judge it only by how shop owners feel about the cut
b.why: The cut helps shops now and may cost drivers later, so the effects differ across time and groups. Each other option looks at only one time or one group, which leaves out part of the picture.
b.clue: Check both when effects occur and who they affect.

a.best: Skipping repairs to save money, then paying bigger bills

b.best: List effects now and later for shops, drivers and ratepayers

problems.detail: The right option is the only one without "Judge it only". The three wrong options repeat that phrase, so a student could pick the answer from the pattern without knowing the idea.
The stem says the council "must later cut road repairs", stating the later cost as certain. The card says effects "may" fall on groups, and the why says the cut "may cost drivers later".

"Borrowing to study costs money now and repayments later" is muddled. Borrowing provides money now; the cost now is the fees or time. In Australia, HECS-HELP loans usually mean no upfront payment, so students may be confused about what the cost now is.

check.summary: Both answers are clear and correct, but in question b the right option stands out because every wrong option says "Judge it only", and the stem says "must" where the card and the why say "may". The card's borrowing example is also worded confusingly about what costs money now.

b.q: A council in Tasmania cuts a local tax to help shops now. It may then have less money for road repairs later. What is the best way to judge the decision?

Count the extra money shops gain in the first year
Look at the state of local roads in ten years
Ask shop owners if they are happy with the tax cut
